metadata.title: Nutrition in Plants
metadata.subject: Science
learning_outcomes: Understand the modes of nutrition in plants (autotrophic and heterotrophic).
Explain the process of photosynthesis and its essential requirements.
Identify alternative modes of nutrition in plants such as parasitic, insectivorous, and saprotrophic.

ai_context.learning_goal: Master how plants obtain and synthesize food, recognizing that all living organisms ultimately depend on plants.
common_misconceptions: Plants get their food from the soil like we get food from plates.
Photosynthesis happens only during the night.

blocks.title: The Great Green Kitchen
blocks.body: Imagine walking into the largest kitchen on Earth—one that doesn't use gas, electricity, or grocery stores. This kitchen uses raw sunlight, invisible air, and water from the dirt beneath our feet to cook meals that feed every single living creature on our planet. From the grass beneath a grasshopper to the majestic oak tree, every plant is a master chef running an invisible, silent factory. Have you ever wondered how a plant cooks its own food without a mouth, a stove, or hands? Let's step inside the microscopic world of plant nutrition and uncover the secret recipe of life.

blocks.question: Where do plants primarily get the raw materials to build their body and create food?
options: Only from the packaged fertilizers we add to the soil
From air, water, and sunlight using internal biological processes
By absorbing fully cooked organic matter directly from neighboring plants
blocks.explanation: Plants utilize simple inorganic substances—carbon dioxide from the air, water from the soil, and energy from sunlight—to manufacture their own food.

blocks.title: What is Nutrition?
blocks.body: All living organisms require food to build their bodies, grow, repair damaged parts, and obtain the energy necessary to carry out life processes. [DICT_C7_AUTOTROPH|Nutrition] is the mode of taking food by an organism and its utilization by the body. Organisms that can make food themselves from simple substances are called [DICT_C7_AUTOTROPH|autotrophs] (auto = self, troph = nourishment). Therefore, plants are called autotrophs. Animals and most other organisms take in food prepared by plants and are called [DICT_C7_HETEROTROPH|heterotrophs] (heteros = other). This fundamental division dictates how life flows across every ecosystem on Earth.

blocks.title: Autotroph vs Heterotroph
blocks.body:
Front: What is the main difference between autotrophs and heterotrophs?

Back: Autotrophs synthesize their own food from simple inorganic materials (like plants), whereas heterotrophs must consume other organisms for nutrition (like animals and humans).

blocks.title: Photosynthesis: Food Making Factory in Plants
blocks.body: If plants are the chefs, [DICT_C7_PHOTOSYNTHESIS|photosynthesis] is their primary recipe. But how does it happen? Water and minerals present in the soil are absorbed by the roots and transported to the leaves. Carbon dioxide from air is taken in through tiny pores present on the surface of leaves. These pores are surrounded by 'guard cells' and are called [DICT_C7_STOMATA|stomata]. Water travels up through vessel-like tubes that run throughout the root, stem, and leaves, acting like a complex plumbing network. Inside the leaves, a green pigment called chlorophyll plays a heroic role. Chlorophyll helps leaves capture the energy of sunlight. This energy is used to synthesize (mix and chemicalize) food from carbon dioxide and water. Because the synthesis of food occurs in the presence of sunlight, it is called photosynthesis (photo = light, synthesis = to combine).

blocks.title: The Stomata Detective
blocks.body: Take a leaf from a potted plant, apply a thin layer of clear nail polish to the underside, let it dry for 5 minutes, peel it off gently with tweezers, and observe it under a school microscope. You will see hundreds of tiny mouth-like structures—these are the stomata through which leaves breathe!

blocks.question: What is the primary function of chlorophyll in green leaves?
options: To absorb water directly from falling raindrops
To capture solar energy from sunlight to drive photosynthesis
To give the plant a sweet taste for herbivores
blocks.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that traps solar energy, which is essential for powering the chemical conversion of carbon dioxide and water into food.
blocks.question_hi: [HINDI] What is the primary function of chlorophyll in green leaves?

blocks.title: The Solar Energy Ultimate Converter
blocks.body: Solar energy is captured by the leaves and stored in the plant in the form of food. Thus, sun is the ultimate source of energy for all living organisms. Can you imagine life on earth in the absence of photosynthesis? Without photosynthesis, there would be no food. The survival of almost all living organisms directly or indirectly depends upon the food made by plants. Besides, oxygen which is essential for the survival of all organisms is produced during photosynthesis. In the absence of photosynthesis, life on earth would be impossible. Oxygen is released as a byproduct during this miraculous chemical reaction, maintaining the breathable atmosphere we enjoy every single day.

blocks.title: The Photosynthesis Equation Check
blocks.body:
Front: What are the necessary inputs and outputs of photosynthesis?

Back: Inputs = Carbon Dioxide + Water + Sunlight (with Chlorophyll). Outputs = Carbohydrates (Food) + Oxygen.

blocks.title: Synthesis of Plant Food Other Than Carbohydrates
blocks.body: You have just learned that plants synthesize carbohydrates through the process of photosynthesis. But carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. These are used to make other components of food such as proteins and fats. Proteins are nitrogenous substances which contain nitrogen. From where do plants obtain nitrogen? Recall that nitrogen is present in abundance in gaseous form in the air. However, plants cannot absorb nitrogen in this gaseous form! Soil has certain bacteria that absorb gaseous nitrogen and convert it into a usable form and release it into the soil. These are absorbed by the plants along with water. You might have also seen farmers adding fertilizers rich in nitrogen to the soil. In this way, plants fulfill their requirements of nitrogen along with the other constituents.

blocks.question: Why can't plants use atmospheric nitrogen directly, even though air is 78% nitrogen?
options: Because nitrogen is toxic to plant leaves
Because plants lack the biochemical machinery to break gaseous nitrogen bonds, requiring soil bacteria to fix it first
Because nitrogen is too heavy to enter through stomata
blocks.explanation: Plants need nitrogen in fixed, usable chemical forms provided by soil bacteria or fertilizers, as they cannot use atmospheric diatomic nitrogen gas directly.

blocks.title: Other Modes of Nutrition in Plants
blocks.body: Not all plants follow the standard textbook recipe of independent photosynthesis. There are some plants which do not have chlorophyll. They cannot synthesize their food. How do they survive and from where do they derive nutrition? Like humans and animals, such plants depend on the food produced by other plants. They use the heterotrophic mode of nutrition. Look at a plant like Cuscuta (Amarbel). It does not have chlorophyll. It takes food from the plant on which it is climbing. The plant on which it climbs is called the host. Since it deprives the host of valuable nutrients, Cuscuta is called a parasite. Nature is full of these fascinating evolutionary adaptations where survival takes remarkably creative paths.

blocks.title: Parasitic Plant Spotting
blocks.body: When walking in a garden or park, look for yellowish, tubular, thread-like structures winding around the stems and branches of trees. That is Cuscuta (Amarbel), a classic example of a total plant parasite stealing food without making any of its own!

A parasite that steals ready-made food from the host
An autotrophic neighbor sharing sunlight

blocks.title: Insectivorous Plants: The Meat-Eaters
blocks.body: Have you ever heard of plants that can eat animals? There are a few plants which can trap insects and digest them. Such plants may be green or of some other color. Look at the pitcher plant! The pitcher-like or jug-like structure is the modified part of the leaf. The apex of the leaf forms a lid which can open and close the mouth of the pitcher. Inside the pitcher, there are hair directed downwards. When an insect lands in the pitcher, the lid closes and the trapped insect gets entangled into the hair. The insect is digested by the digestive juices secreted in the pitcher and its nutrients are absorbed. Such insect-eating plants are called insectivorous plants. Why do they eat insects if they are green? These plants generally grow in nitrogen-deficient soils, so they supplement their nitrogen intake by trapping and digesting insects!

blocks.title: Why do Pitcher Plants Eat Insects?
blocks.body:
Front: If pitcher plants have green leaves and can perform photosynthesis, why do they eat insects?

Back: They grow in soils that are deficient in nitrogen. Catching and digesting insects provides them with the essential nitrogen they cannot get from the poor soil.

blocks.title: Saprotrophs: Nature's Recycling Crew
blocks.body: You might have seen packets of mushrooms sold in the vegetable market. You may have also seen fluffy umbrella-like patches growing on rotting wood during the rainy season. Let us find out what type of food they need to survive and from where they get it. Fungi appear on rotting organic matter like old bread left in humid weather. They secrete digestive juices on the dead and decaying matter and convert it into a solution and then absorb nutrients from it. This mode of nutrition in which organisms take in nutrients in solution form from dead and decaying matter is called [DICT_C7_SAPROFEEDER|saprotrophic nutrition]. Plants which use saprotrophic nutrition are called [DICT_C7_SAPROFEEDER|saprotrophs]. Fungi also grow on pickles, leather, clothes and other articles that are left in hot and humid weather for long times. During the rainy season, they-spores germinate and multiply rapidly.

blocks.title: Fungal Spore Experiment
blocks.body: Leave a piece of bread moistened with water in a warm, humid place for 2-3 days. Examine the fluffy patches under a magnifying glass or microscope. You will see cotton-like threads spread across the bread and tiny dot-like structures containing spores!

blocks.question: How do saprotrophic fungi obtain their nutrients from dead and decaying matter?
options: By chewing and swallowing solid organic tissue with tiny teeth
By secreting digestive juices onto dead matter to dissolve it into a solution, then absorbing the nutrients
By performing rapid photosynthesis underground
blocks.explanation: Saprotrophs break down dead organic matter externally by secreting digestive juices and absorbing the resulting nutrient solution.

blocks.title: Symbiosis: Living Together and Helping Each Other
blocks.body: Some organisms live together and share both shelter and nutrients. This relationship is called symbiosis. For example, certain fungi live inside the roots of trees. The tree provides nutrients to the fungus and, in return, the fungus provides water and certain nutrients back to the tree. In organisms called lichens, a chlorophyll-containing partner, which is an alga, and a fungus live together. The fungus provides shelter, water and minerals to the alga and, in return, the alga prepares and provides food to the fungus. This cooperative masterclass of biology proves that competition is not the only rule of nature—cooperation builds empires of life across harsh environments.

blocks.title: How Nutrients are Replenished in the Soil
blocks.body: Have you ever seen farmers spreading manure or fertilizers in the fields, or gardeners using them in lawns or in pots? Do you know why they are added to the soil? Recall that plants absorb minerals and nutrients from the soil. So, their amounts in the soil keep on declining. Fertilizers and manures contain plant nutrients such as nitrogen, potassium, phosphorous, etc. These nutrients need to be added from time to time to enrich the soil. Agriculture requires careful management of soil fertility. Without replenishment, crop yields drop dramatically as soil gets depleted of vital elements.

Recall that plants absorb minerals and nutrients from the soil. So, their amounts in the soil keep on declining. Fertilizers and manures contain plant nutrients such as nitrogen, potassium, phosphorous, etc. These nutrients need to be added from time to time to enrich the soil. Agriculture requires careful management of soil fertility. Without replenishment, crop yields drop dramatically as soil gets depleted of vital elements.

blocks.title: The Role of Rhizobium Bacteria in Soil Enrichment
blocks.body: The bacterium called Rhizobium can take atmospheric nitrogen and convert it into a usable form. But Rhizobium cannot make its own food. So it often lives in the roots of gram, peas, moong, beans and other legumes and provides them with nitrogen. In return, the plants provide food and shelter to the bacteria. Thus, they have a symbiotic relationship. This association is of great significance for farmers. They do not need to add nitrogen fertilizer to soil in which leguminous plants are grown. Nature provides an organic, self-sustaining fertilizer factory right inside plant root nodules!

blocks.question: Why do farmers often grow leguminous crops (like peas or beans) in rotation with other crops?
options: Because legumes taste sweeter than other crops
Because root nodules contain Rhizobium bacteria that naturally replenish nitrogen in the soil
Because legumes require zero water to grow

blocks.title: Chapter Synthesis: The Web of Nutritional Interdependence
blocks.body: Most plants are autotrophs. Only a few plants are parasitic or saprotrophic. They derive nutrition from other organisms. All animals are categorized as heterotrophs since they depend on plants and other animals for nutrition. Can we say that the insectivorous plants are partial heterotrophs? Looking across the entire plant kingdom, we witness a stunning variety of nutritional strategies—from the sun-capturing autotrophs powering global ecosystems to clever parasites, meat-eating pitcher plants, and decomposer fungi recycling life's raw materials back into the earth.
